title: Quick start
description: Use the doona interface embedded in honk without downloading separate UI files.
text: Quick start Use the doona interface embedded in honk without downloading separate UI files. Check the gateway requirements first. Keep your existing honk configuration; for a new backend, prepare honk's minimal configuration before adding the API block below. 1. Get honk On 64-bit OpenWrt or ImmortalWrt 25.12, install honk from the daeuniverse feed. On other Linux systems, follow Install honk and choose an archive whose name contains full from honk releases. 2. Configure honk The daeuniverse OpenWrt feed already ships this block, listening on the LAN instead of 127.0.0.1; skip to step 3. Elsewhere, add this block to the honk configuration, replacing any existing native_api block: To run doona lite instead, set ui: 'embedded-lite' (available from honk v0.1.0-beta.4); see doona lite. For other options, see Configuration. Start or restart honk to apply the change. 3. Open doona On the machine running honk, open http://127.0.0.1:9527/. With the OpenWrt feed's default configuration, open http://<router LAN IP>:9527/ from a computer on the LAN, for example http://192.168.1.1:9527/. Use the IP address; honk refuses host names such as openwrt.lan. For another router that listens on 127.0.0.1, run this command on your computer, replacing <router> with its SSH address, and keep the connection open: Open the same URL on your computer. The first visit creates the administrator; see First sign-in.

title: Standard edition and doona lite
description: The standard edition manages configuration and observes traffic.
text: Standard edition and doona lite The standard edition manages configuration and observes traffic. Choose it for traffic dashboards, connection controls, logs, advanced routing traces or editing multiple configuration sources. doona lite focuses on configuration: nodes, subscriptions, groups, routing, DNS and global settings. Choose it for task-specific forms, sharing manual nodes and reviewing configuration drafts without traffic pages. honk also has a Clash-compatible API for Clash dashboards such as zashboard; doona does not use it (see honk's minimal configuration). Compare features Features depend on the resources and permissions honk advertises. Changing editions cannot enable an unavailable backend capability. Feature Standard edition doona lite Traffic monitoring Activity, System status, Connections, Routing log, Logs and Events No traffic pages Widgets Activity widgets and floating or docked widgets No Close connections; export events Yes No Routing tests Rules → Trace simulation, with advanced traffic fields and resolution options Routing → Test rules, with matched rules and outbounds; uses the same routing trace API DNS queries, Resolution log, Statistics and Cache Yes No standalone query or observation pages; routing tests use DNS resolution Nodes, subscriptions and group selection Yes; groups are under Policies Yes; separate Nodes, Subscriptions and Groups pages Multi-line share-link import Yes Yes, through Add node → Paste links Share links and QR codes No dedicated sharing dialog Manual nodes and subscription links; no sharing of subscription nodes Rename a subscription Yes, with an option to update group references No; the name stays fixed after creation Group editing Group form and full source editor Group form, group text editor, duplicate group and copy members between groups Routing and DNS rules Forms and full source editor Forms, reorder controls and per-page visual/text modes DNS upstream presets Edit upstreams in the source editor; no preset form Custom upstreams and Ali DNS, DNSPod and Cloudflare presets Global settings Configuration → Global settings Settings dialog; restart-only values are read-only with Copy Configuration sources Select and edit main/include sources; create sources and inspect diagnostics Edits main only; no full source editor Export configuration Export the selected source Export the applied main or the current page’s unsaved draft Backend management Multiple profiles, sign-out, temporary runtime overrides and geodata management No corresponding management screens Server configuration backups and revisions Available when honk advertises the x-honk extensions No Themes and sign-in Light/dark themes and palettes; administrator credentials or token Light, dark or system theme, no palette selector; same honk credentials Backend requirements Use the native-API honk build in Requirements. Both editions discover authentication through GET /api and read GET /api/v1/capabilities; password mode uses POST /api/v1/auth/setup or POST /api/v1/auth/login. The features below require other endpoints; not every connection needs them. Paths in this table start with /api/v1. Feature honk resources and endpoints Editions Configuration editing config read/write, config_validate and operations; GET /config, POST /config/validate, PUT /config/sources/{source_id}, GET /operations/{operation_id} Both; lite requires full validation and complete, hash-matching, writable main content. Standard source editing validates when supported. lite’s share-link import also needs syntax validation. Nodes, subscriptions and groups nodes, providers, groups; GET /nodes, GET /providers, GET /groups, GET /groups/{group_id}, POST /providers/{provider_id}/refresh, PUT/DELETE /groups/{group_id}/selection; probes via POST /probes Both; lite edits declarations through main source replacement. The standard edition also uses node/provider create/delete and group configuration endpoints. Status and service commands runtime, operations, and the advertised reload/suspend/resume capabilities. Endpoints: GET /runtime, GET /version (standard edition), POST /operations/reload, /operations/suspend, /operations/resume, plus operation polling Both; lite uses status in the shell rather than a traffic dashboard. Routing tests routing_trace via POST /routing/trace; rules via GET /rules; dns_query via POST /dns/query for name resolution when needed Both; honk’s resolution modes determine the available tests. Traffic and DNS observations traffic_history, memory_history, runtime_memory, runtime_outbounds, datapath, connections, flows, events, logs, dns_log, dns_cache, dns_query; GET /runtime/traffic/history, /runtime/memory/history, /runtime/memory, /runtime/outbounds, /datapath, /connections, /flows, /events, /logs, /dns/log, /dns/cache, /dns/rules, plus POST /dns/query and connection/cache deletion when writable Standard edition Source and backend management POST /config/sources; geodata via GET /geodata and POST /geodata/update; runtime_settings via GET/PATCH /runtime/settings; POST /auth/logout Standard edition Server backups and revisions The advertised x-honk configuration export/import/revisions extensions, under /x-honk/config/ Standard edition; requires those extensions, beyond the base contract lite reuses the standard edition’s src/api/client.ts and models backed by the generated src/api/types.ts; it has its own UI and state. The OpenAPI contract defines the endpoint schemas. See common lite tasks for the editing prerequisites in user terms. Install and switch editions Use Quick start for the embedded standard edition, doona lite to switch to lite, or install UI files separately to serve a directory. honk serves one edition at /ui/ at a time. Select its embedded UI or directory with experimental.native_api.ui, then restart honk, not just reload. The manual installation guide gives each edition a separate archive and directory, so installing one does not overwrite the other. To use both at once, let honk serve one edition and use a static server for the other directory. Allow the second origin as described in hostname and origin access. Browser settings Both editions share honk's native API, configuration and configuration changes. Each edition keeps its browser settings separately. Demos Try the standard edition demo or the doona lite demo.

title: Requirements
description: Check the gateway and browser before installing doona and honk.
text: Requirements Check the gateway and browser before installing doona and honk. For an individual page or action, use Feature requirements. Gateway Follow honk’s Linux kernel requirements and bpffs setup before starting the backend. Component Requirement Operating system Linux; run the real transparent-proxy backend as root. Kernel Linux 6.12 or later; the real eBPF backend rejects older kernels. cgroup cgroup v2 with BPF support; the required socket hooks must attach. Kernel type information Raw BTF matching the running kernel, not an ELF debug image. BPF filesystem bpffs mounted at /sys/fs/bpf for the default pin directory. HTTPS downloads A system CA certificate store from your distribution. Keep console access or another way into the gateway for the first real start: honk changes its networking. Check these kernel options using the commands in the linked honk guide: The real backend needs CONFIG_BPF=y, CONFIG_BPF_SYSCALL=y, CONFIG_BPF_JIT=y, CONFIG_CGROUP_BPF=y, CONFIG_NET_SCHED=y, CONFIG_NET_CLS_ACT=y, CONFIG_NET_XGRESS=y and CONFIG_NET_NS=y. CONFIG_NET_CLS_ACT selects CONFIG_NET_XGRESS. The TCX backend does not require the legacy CONFIG_NET_CLS_BPF or CONFIG_NET_SCH_INGRESS options. The default held-first-packet UDP path also needs CONFIG_NF_TABLES, CONFIG_NF_TABLES_INET, CONFIG_NFT_CT, CONFIG_NFT_QUEUE and CONFIG_NETFILTER_NETLINK_QUEUE, each set to y or m. honk reads raw BTF from HONK_VMLINUX_BTF if set. Otherwise it tries /sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux, then /usr/lib/debug/boot/vmlinux; OpenWrt's vmlinux-btf package supplies the latter. Confirm that /sys/fs/bpf is a bpffs mountpoint, not just a directory. If the system does not mount it automatically, use the /etc/fstab entry in honk's bpffs instructions above. honk version Use a honk build that implements doona's native API contract and includes the native-api build feature. A version number alone does not establish compatibility. Without that feature, a build cannot serve the API even with its configuration block. Choose a compatible honk-core archive using the installation guide. The app's contract pin identifies the API it expects. On the gateway, run: After signing in, compare the running engine version on System status with the installed binary. For a missing API or a rejected build, see native API troubleshooting. Browser and source builds Component Requirement Browser Standard-edition build targets: Chrome or Edge 120, Firefox 121, Safari 17 or later; JavaScript target ES2022. Build the app Node ^22.13.0 || ^24.0.0 || >=26.0.0 and pnpm 11.15.1. Build this documentation site Node ^22.18.0 || ^24.0.0 || >=26.0.0 and pnpm 11.15.1. Node and pnpm are only needed for development, not to serve a prebuilt interface. Process-name routing has additional feature requirements.

Install net-misc/curl and app-misc/ca-certificates if they are missing. 1. Prepare a local repository If you already have a local repository, set REPO to its absolute path and skip the creation commands. Otherwise, create a new repository named doona-local: The repository name must appear in the final command’s output. 2. Add the ebuild 3. Verify the release archives The ebuild uses the program archive and enables the fonts USE flag by default. In your download directory, fetch and verify both archives: Continue only when every selected file reports OK. title: Install on OpenWrt
description: Install doona v0.1.0-rc.4 and honk on an OpenWrt router.
headings: Quick install from the daeuniverse feed
1. Check the router and prepare tools
text: Install on OpenWrt Install doona v0.1.0-rc.4 and honk on an OpenWrt router. Run every command in a root shell on the router and keep the same shell open throughout the installation. Quick install from the daeuniverse feed On supported 64-bit OpenWrt or ImmortalWrt 25.12 routers, install honk from the daeuniverse feed, then follow Quick start to configure its embedded doona. The steps below are the manual archive route, an alternative for routers the feed does not support. The feed package and the manual route use different service names and data directories; choose one route. 1. Check the router and prepare tools Check the backend prerequisites, including the kernel, BTF, cgroup, and CPU requirements, before downloading. A matching doona package does not establish that the router can run honk. Check storage for installed files and the download directory: OpenWrt 25.12 uses apk-tools 3; OpenWrt 24.10 and earlier use opkg and ipk packages. Stock OpenWrt 24.10 uses Linux 6.6, below honk’s minimum kernel requirement linked above. Installing a matching UI package does not resolve that incompatibility. Choose the commands for the router’s package manager. OpenWrt provides the veth module and NFQUEUE modules as packages: If NFQUEUE lacks prerequisites despite its enabled setting, honk can continue running without NFQUEUE staging and issue a startup warning. Check the service log; successful service startup does not confirm active NFQUEUE staging. 2. Download and verify doona These packages install the standard edition. For lite, use the archive route in manual installation, omitting sudo, then return at step 4. Download into /tmp/doona and choose the package format used by the firmware. The OpenWrt apk packages are separate from Alpine’s packages. /tmp uses RAM and loses its contents at reboot. Allow space for both the downloaded honk archive and its extracted directory at the same time. Continue only when every selected file reports OK. If verification fails or finds no checksum line, check the filenames and download again before installing. For download or binary errors, see Installation errors. 3. Install the package For apk, install the verified public key and use the signed index. Keep the index and package files in the same directory. Without the release key and index, you can install a verified local apk directly: This skips signature trust checking, so verify the package’s SHA-256 entry before using this alternative. The last command must list index.html. Use the separate UI configuration with this directory. Optional packages Choose optional assets only if you need them. Download the chosen file into /tmp/doona and verify its individual entry in SHA256SUMS as in step 2. Package apk filename opkg filename doona-fonts doona-fonts-0.1.0_rc4-r1.apk doona-fonts_0.1.0-rc.4-1_all.ipk doona-precompressed doona-precompressed-0.1.0_rc4-r1.apk doona-precompressed_0.1.0-rc.4-1_all.ipk For apk, repeat the install command with the chosen package name instead of doona. For opkg, set FILE to the chosen filename and repeat the install command. 4. Install honk Follow Install honk in a separate download directory so its SHA256SUMS does not replace doona’s. Choose a musl build and the OpenWrt installation tab, which installs /usr/bin/honk-core. Then return here. After verifying the installed binary, remove its downloaded archive and extracted directory using their absolute paths. Once you have installed all chosen optional UI packages, remove the downloaded doona packages, index, key copy, and checksums from /tmp/doona using their absolute paths. Keep any downloads still needed for installation. 5. Prepare the data directory For this manual route, set global.data_dir to /etc/honk/data in the honk configuration, then prepare the persistent directory: Only download geodata when your rules need it; see geodata requirements. For this layout: Alternatively, install the distribution’s v2ray geodata packages instead of downloading the files above: honk searches /usr/share/dae, but not /usr/share/v2ray directly. Check for existing files or links under /usr/share/dae; create any missing links as follows: Files already present in the configured data directory take precedence over these packaged files. Use the OpenWrt service in Service management, not the feed service. Preserve configuration across sysupgrade Before a normal sysupgrade that preserves configuration, add these paths to /etc/sysupgrade.conf if they are not already listed, then check the backup list: Confirm that the list includes your honk configuration, data files, and init script. This configuration backup does not restore installed kernel modules, /usr/bin/honk-core, or /usr/share/doona. After upgrading, repeat steps 1–4 to reinstall the tools, kernel modules, UI packages, and honk binary. If you chose packaged geodata, reinstall it and recreate its links using step 5. Keep the restored configuration and data, then enable and start the service. Check the service log, then follow First sign-in.

Install the binary For a new installation, choose the tab for your shell. For an update, stop the existing service first using Service management, then replace the binary. The version command must run successfully. Keep the downloaded release name with your installation records. For an update, keep the existing configuration and restart the service. Check that its startup log reports the installed engine version. If you arrived from a distribution guide, return there to finish. Build from source instead Follow honk’s source-build instructions for the toolchains, eBPF build, and BTF check. From the honk repository root, replace its final honk-core build command with: ebpf supplies the real datapath; native-api supplies doona’s API. Install target/release/honk-core at the binary path above. Release binaries embed the eBPF object, so you need not install a separate object file. GLIBC_* not found when starting honk The selected gnu binary requires a newer glibc. Choose the matching static musl build from honk’s release. BusyBox rejects --ignore-missing BusyBox sha256sum does not support that option. Use the per-file awk and sha256sum -c - command shown in these installation guides. Require an OK result for the selected file. Install geodata when your rules need it Check geodata requirements before adding Geo rules. Use the data directory selected in your configuration. For the /var/lib/honk layout used by the systemd guide, run: In a root shell, omit sudo. On OpenWrt, use its geodata steps. For later updates and their conditions, see geodata updates. Install the UI files Follow the distribution guide above or manual installation. Use the directory containing index.html for the ui setting: Installation UI directory Debian or Ubuntu package /usr/share/doona-web Other packages or the standard archive instructions /usr/share/doona Lite archive instructions /usr/share/doona-lite Optional assets Asset Purpose doona-fonts Noto Sans TC and SC fonts for the standard edition. doona-precompressed .br and .gz copies beside the standard edition’s files for servers that serve precompressed assets. Use the same release as the main package. Debian names these doona-web-fonts and doona-web-precompressed. Package filenames are on each distribution page; archive steps are under manual installation. Precompressed assets use additional disk space; omit them on routers with limited storage. Without the optional font archive, doona uses fallback fonts and does not load the optional font faces. It still requests fonts/README to detect the archive’s presence. Local builds and packaging recipes The repository supplies OpenWrt, Alpine, Gentoo and Nix recipes, not yet submitted to their distribution repositories. The AUR doona-bin recipe has a separate repository. For a staged installation, first complete a local build. From the doona repository root, run these commands, replacing /absolute/staging/path with your staging directory. Both targets accept DESTDIR and PREFIX; omit the second command if you do not need fonts. The commands install the UI files under the staging directory’s usr/share/doona. Serve the UI through another address Use the native API settings for listener, UI directory, Host, and Origin configuration. Check sign-in requirements before using a hostname or reverse proxy. Hostnames and static-file 403 errors For http://owrt.lan:9527/ui/, add these entries inside the existing experimental.native_api block, retaining its other settings and allowlist entries: allowed_hosts takes a hostname and port without a scheme or path. allow_origins takes the scheme, hostname and port without a path or trailing slash. For multiple entries, quote each separately and separate them with commas, as in allowed_hosts: 'owrt.lan:9527', 'router.lan:9527'. Do not use JSON brackets or quote the whole list. Allowing a Host does not automatically allow its Origin. If HTML loads but JavaScript or CSS returns 403, inspect the failing requests in the browser’s Network panel. Compare Host and Origin, including their ports, with the allowlists. After editing them, restart honk and reload the page. Static servers and reverse proxies A static server can serve the extracted UI files at its web root or under a prefix such as /ui/. doona uses hash routes such as /ui/#/activity, so it needs no SPA rewrite rules. Forward both the exact /api discovery endpoint and the /api/ subtree to honk’s listener. Forwarding /api/ alone misses discovery and prevents connection. If the connection address has a proxy prefix such as /gateway, route /gateway/api to honk’s /api and /gateway/api/… to /api/…. Apply the same prefix mapping to both routes. Maintain the installation Reload or restart Use What doona can change to determine how an edit takes effect, then use the commands in Service management. Update the UI For an external UI directory, install the new package or archive using the same installation method. Replacing files in the already configured directory needs only a browser reload. With ui: embedded, a standalone UI package does not replace the embedded interface. Either update honk to a build containing the newer UI using Install honk, or install the UI files separately and change ui to their directory. Restart honk after either change, then reload the browser page. After installing the UI files, apply the configuration at the start of this page, restart honk, and follow First sign-in.

title: Service management
description: Configure honk with Quick start or the separate UI setup, then use this page to manage a manually installed service and read its logs.
text: Service management Configure honk with Quick start or the separate UI setup, then use this page to manage a manually installed service and read its logs. For a feed installation, use the feed’s service instructions instead; do not create a second service. 1. Create the service Choose the section for your service manager. If a honk service already exists, inspect its executable and configuration paths before replacing it. The examples below use the paths from this site’s installation guides. systemd Run on the gateway. In a root shell, omit sudo. This unit uses /usr/local/bin/honk-core and /etc/honk/config.dae. The unit follows honk’s systemd example. Check that guide before adding privilege restrictions to the service. OpenWrt procd Run as root on the router. This script uses /usr/bin/honk-core and the data directory prepared by OpenWrt installation. MIMALLOC_PURGE_DELAY=0 requests immediate purging from mimalloc. See honk’s CLI reference for this setting. 2. Enable and start honk For systemd, look for active (running). On OpenWrt, the status should report running. Open doona as described in Quick start to confirm that the listener is reachable. Check the current startup log for native API listener ready and honk-core is running. At the API listener's /api address, a JSON response whose auth object has setup_required set to true means the API is reachable and no administrator exists yet. API access alone does not prove that the real eBPF backend can route traffic. Read startup diagnostics even when honk starts successfully: the parser warns about and ignores unknown scalar keys in global. Read the logs To follow new messages, use sudo journalctl -u honk-core -f on systemd or logread -f -e honk-core on OpenWrt. Press Ctrl+C to stop following. If startup fails, use the error in the log with Troubleshooting. The journal includes earlier service runs. Diagnose the current start from the latest honk-core … starting message, which also reports the engine version. Reload, restart, or stop Check What doona can change before choosing reload or restart. After either command, read the log to confirm the result. Task systemd OpenWrt Start sudo systemctl start honk-core /etc/init.d/honk-core start Reload configuration sudo systemctl reload honk-core /etc/init.d/honk-core reload Restart sudo systemctl restart honk-core /etc/init.d/honk-core restart Stop sudo systemctl stop honk-core /etc/init.d/honk-core stop Disable startup at boot sudo systemctl disable honk-core /etc/init.d/honk-core disable Disabling startup at boot does not stop a running service. To keep honk stopped after reboot, run both stop and disable. Service and reload errors Symptom or log message Meaning and next step systemd cannot find honk-core.service Create the unit using step 1, run sudo systemctl daemon-reload, then start it using step 2. Reload reports no running honk-core instance No real instance holds the process lock. A foreground process using --mock-ebpf does not hold that lock. Start the intended real service using step 2. SIGHUP reload applied honk applied the new configuration. SIGHUP reload rejected Read the accompanying stage and errors to determine whether honk applied the new configuration. For a restart-required rejection, edit the listed settings on the host and restart honk. SIGHUP reload committed with degraded datapath honk committed the configuration, but the datapath remains degraded. Read the accompanying errors before treating the service as healthy. A successful reload command alone does not prove that honk applied the configuration; check the service log for the outcome. OpenRC or a foreground test This page does not provide an OpenRC service script. After configuring honk, stop any existing instance before running it in a terminal to complete the first sign-in: Keep the terminal open and use the browser steps in Quick start. Logs appear in the terminal; Ctrl+C stops honk. This command does not enable startup at boot. Stop the foreground process before starting the service. If you use --mock-ebpf for a startup check, it does not test real eBPF attachment or routing. Expect the warning NFQUEUE is unavailable at startup; continuing with NFQUEUE staging disabled when its reason is the mock eBPF backend was selected.

title: Route your first connection
description: Continue from Quick start, with honk running and your administrator signed in.
headings: 3. Send the test domain through the group
5. Add the DNS rule and apply it
6. Verify the rule with Trace simulation
text: Route your first connection Continue from Quick start, with honk running and your administrator signed in. You need a working HTTP or HTTPS subscription URL and shell access to the gateway. This exercise sends example.com through a new group named proxy and leaves other traffic direct. Use harbor for the subscription name. Start with a direct-only configuration: fallback: direct, no DNS block, and no existing harbor subscription or proxy group. Keep API credentials in a separate include so the main file remains editable; see the configuration example. At this point, example.com uses the direct fallback. After adding the proxy rule in step 3, verify in step 6 that its outbound is proxy. 1. Add the subscription Open Nodes and select Add subscription. Enter harbor in Name and your provider's URL in Subscription URL, then select Add. doona writes the declaration and requests a refresh. Check that the success notice reports nodes and that selecting harbor lists its nodes. If doona saved the declaration but the fetch failed, resolve the reported error, then use Update harbor on its card. Continue only when the subscription has proxy nodes. For disabled controls, check node and subscription requirements or refresh requirements. 2. Create the group Open Policies and select New group. Enter proxy in Group name. Set Selection policy to Fastest on average. In Subscriptions, select harbor and check Matching nodes before selecting Create. The proxy card must appear with the subscription's members. Expand it to inspect the selected member and its latency or health status. Do not continue with an empty group. For disabled controls, see group creation and editing requirements. 3. Send the test domain through the group Open Rules → Routing rules. Select Advanced if the view switch appears, then Add rule. Field Value Condition form Select Match by Full domain Values example.com Outbound proxy Insert Last, before the fallback Select Add rule in the dialog. This writes and reloads immediately. Check the notice New rule is in effect and the new rule: Keep fallback: direct. If you cannot add a rule, see routing rule requirements. 4. Define a DNS upstream Open Configuration → Config files, select /etc/honk/config.dae in Config file, and append the following block after the existing sections. Keep the subscription, group and routing rule you just created. Select Apply. Wait for the notice confirming the file write and configuration reload. Reopen the file and check that remote_dns is present. For a disabled editor or Apply button, see configuration write requirements. 5. Add the DNS rule and apply it Open Rules → DNS rules. In Request rules, select Add rule. Set Match by to Full domain, enter example.com in Values, choose remote_dns in Action, and set Insert to Last, before the fallback. Select Add rule to write and reload. Check New rule is in effect and the request rule: The routing rule chooses the traffic's group; the DNS rule chooses the resolver whose requests use that group. Each save above applies separately. If you cannot add a rule, see DNS rule requirements. 6. Verify the rule with Trace simulation On Rules, open Trace simulation. Set Network protocol to TCP, Domain to example.com, and Destination port to 443. Leave Destination IP empty, choose No resolution (none) in Resolution mode, and select Run trace. The result must match your domain rule and show proxy as the outbound, with a node from harbor in the node chain. Repeat with example.net: its outbound must be direct. Trace simulates rule evaluation; it does not open a connection or prove that the proxy can reach the website. For disabled controls, see routing trace requirements. 7. Observe a real connection Open Connections before making the request. On the gateway, run: While it transfers, look for example.com on Connections and open its row. Check that the chain uses proxy and one of harbor's nodes. Short connections can finish before you inspect them; repeat the request if necessary. A successful transfer confirms that the route carries real traffic. For an unavailable page, see connection requirements. honk handles proxied traffic in userspace, so it appears in Connections. The kernel forwards direct traffic, which does not appear there. Use Trace to inspect the direct fallback, and the configuration reference for the complete file example.

title: First sign-in
description: Connect the standard edition to a running honk, create its administrator if needed, and check the backend status.
text: First sign-in Connect the standard edition to a running honk, create its administrator if needed, and check the backend status. Complete Service management first; lite users should follow Connect doona lite. 1. Open the interface From the gateway or a device on its LAN, open http://192.168.1.1:9527/ui/, replacing the address with your gateway's API listener address. For a hostname or a separately hosted interface, follow hostname and origin access. With no saved backend profile, the interface discovers the API at the hosting address. If the form points at the wrong backend, select Change backend URL. Check sign-in requirements if discovery or authentication is unavailable. Before signing in, use the upper-right controls to change the language, palette and color scheme. 2. Follow the form you see Form Action Create the administrator Enter Username, Password and Confirm password, then select Create and sign in. Sign in Enter the existing administrator's Username and Password, then select Sign in. Token required Enter the backend's configured secret in Token, then select Connect. For a new account, the username must contain 1 to 64 ASCII letters, digits, underscores, periods or hyphens. The password must contain 8 to 128 characters, and its confirmation must match. In token mode, use the Token field's show/hide control to check the entered secret before connecting.  3. Check the backend Open System status. On a phone, choose Activity in the bottom bar first. Check the lifecycle status and the Engine card. Confirm that the engine is honk and the version is the build you installed. Inspect Backend features. Use feature requirements to interpret unavailable controls. Continue with Route your first connection to add a subscription and test a proxy route, or use the interface tour to find a page. If sign-in fails Symptom Next step The browser cannot open the page Run curl http://192.168.1.1:9527/api on the gateway, replacing the IP. If it works there but the LAN browser cannot connect, check whether the gateway firewall blocks port 9527. If it fails on the gateway too, check the service and listener in Service management. The form reports no native API Check honk version. honk refuses administrator setup Check the allowed client addresses under sign-in requirements. honk rejects credentials or you forgot the password Follow sign-in troubleshooting. See Configuration for authentication keys. Do not put a password or token in a screenshot or issue report.

title: Interface tour
description: Find pages and controls in the standard edition after signing in.
headings: Use search and the top bar
Understand a write before confirming it
text: Interface tour Find pages and controls in the standard edition after signing in. For the smaller interface, use Common tasks in doona lite. Find a page You want to Open See traffic summaries or backend status Activity or System status Inspect individual connections and routing decisions Connections or Routing log Inspect DNS, diagnostic messages or backend events DNS, Logs or Events Choose a group member or manage nodes and rules Policies, Nodes or Rules Edit configuration sources Configuration Change browser preferences or use backend controls Settings If a page or action is unavailable, check its feature requirements. Press ? to open the keyboard shortcut list. Press g, then a page letter within 800 ms, to open that page. For example, g then r opens Rules.  Use search and the top bar Control Use Search, Ctrl K or ⌘K Find pages, settings and actions. Selecting a result opens its destination. Refresh or r Reread displayed data; Data refreshed. confirms completion. Does not write configuration or reload honk. Reload honk Request a configuration reload after confirmation; see reload requirements. Held-rule count Apply the rules you have held; see held rules. Theme, Language, Palette Change the interface's appearance or language. The held-rule apply button reports the rule count; its label includes the file count for writes to more than one file. Applying held rules and reloading honk disable each other while either action is running. When the theme follows the system, the theme button selects the opposite color scheme; pressing it again returns to System. The Palette menu ends with Appearance settings, which opens the Appearance tab containing Wordmark. Select the backend indicator in the sidebar to inspect the connection and engine version. Its popover also shows the API, Backend URL and saved profile, if any. Edit backend opens backend settings; About doona opens version details. Use panels Inspect a row Open Connections, Routing log or DNS and select a row. Read its details beside the list at widths of at least 1200 px, or in a drawer at narrower widths. Use More actions for additional commands where available. Select Close or press Esc to return to the list. Tabs under a page title switch views within that page. For traffic fields and filters, see Watching traffic. Arrange the floating panel Open Panel options → Edit widgets. In the three-column layout, the preview, gallery and settings scroll separately. Select a Speed widget to change Combine upload and download charts. The switch appears for medium or large widgets using Sparkline. Turn it off for separate charts. Each widget keeps its own choice, including a saved split-chart choice. Select Save to store the layout in this browser. Action Result Pin panel Locks the position and size, including dragging, arrow-key movement, resizing and dragging into the sidebar. Unpin panel restores these actions. Change pages An unpinned floating panel collapses. Both traffic rates remain visible, even in a narrow panel. Hide at edge Hides a floating, unpinned panel at the window edge; both traffic rates remain visible on its handle. Undock Returns a docked panel to floating mode. The docked header has no title, and this button replaces the pin button. Resize A floating panel with no saved size is 280 px wide; you can narrow it to 200 px. Horizontal resizing lets its height grow with the content within the window. Resizing the top or bottom edge preserves the chosen height. For widget types and dashboard layouts, see Widgets. Understand a write before confirming it A button's meaning depends on the control beside it. See held rules for rule Hold and Apply. Compare source writes, runtime changes and browser preferences in What doona can change. Check the result Read the success or failure notification after an action. Reopen the edited resource and check its value. For a routing change, follow the tutorial's trace and connection checks. If honk refuses a source write, use read-only sources and write failures. Check when changes take effect before retrying or restarting. Press Enter in a single-line field to submit the sign-in form, runtime settings or the node, subscription, check, profile-name, custom-geodata-URL, rule and routing-template dialogs. While a modal dialog is open, notifications appear at the top center regardless of the saved notification position, with the dialog below them. Tables, cards, charts and forms use placeholders while loading; sign-in and search use spinners. A button waiting longer than one second shows a spinner while retaining its size. Navigate on a phone Below 1024 px, the bottom bar and page strip replace the sidebar. Choose a section in the bottom bar, then a page in the strip. Each section reopens the page last visited in that section during this browser session. Search, Refresh and the held-rule apply button remain in the top bar. More options contains reload, language, theme, palette and backend controls. Page toolbars keep their first action visible and move the remaining actions into overflow. Below 600 px, pages use the phone spacing and wrapping layout.

title: Watching traffic
description: Choose a monitoring view and check what its data covers in the standard edition.
text: Watching traffic Choose a monitoring view and check what its data covers in the standard edition. For step-by-step checks, see common tasks; for the smaller edition, see doona lite. What you need Where to look Current traffic and engine health Activity Backend version, warnings or a missing feature System status A live connection's route Connections Recorded routing decisions Routing log DNS answers, cache or resolution history DNS Engine messages Logs Configuration and runtime events Events Activity Activity combines traffic, connection, latency and system cards. If setup is incomplete, Getting started links to the remaining setup tasks; use the tutorial to complete them. Each step completes automatically when its condition is met: A subscription or proxy node exists. Routing has been chosen. A group's selected proxy node has a successful latency result. Completing all steps or dismissing the card hides it; this browser remembers that state.  Card or control How to read it Outbound mode and Global outbound Follow switching mode to change them. Download and Upload Open the traffic view on Connections. Read any coverage warning before treating the values as totals for the gateway. Active connections Opens the connection list. Latency Follows a policy group's selected node. CPU usage Opens System status. Top devices and domains Ranks the returned connection sample. Notifications Combines repeated notices and shows their repeat count. Unavailable history or metrics depend on runtime status and history recording. Select Latency to open its node on Nodes. Automatic follows the policy group with the most active connections; a manual group choice is kept in this browser and affects only this card. CPU and latency trends need two samples. Failed latency probes leave gaps, and changing the selection restarts its series. Muted runtime figures retain the last successful reading while a read is failing. The notification badge counts distinct folded notices, not their repeat counts. Stream ready remains on Events. A flow gap with reason recording_changed and no specific record marks a recording-history boundary; it does not necessarily mean records were lost. Change the startup page under Appearance; Show trends on activity cards there controls activity-card trends. Use Edit dashboard to add, move, resize or remove cards. Done saves the layout. To discard edits, select Cancel and confirm. Layout storage has browser requirements. You can place each widget at most three times. Available sizes depend on the widget, and resizing one card does not resize its neighbors. Removing a card offers Undo while the editor remains open. The gallery includes Subscription quota, Outbound failures, Node availability and DNS latency. Memory can use a chart or a Sparkline value tile. Wide charts show peak and average statistics beside the chart. See Widgets for the shared dashboard and floating-panel gallery.  System status Check the backend on System status before diagnosing an unavailable feature. The header shows engine state, Config version, Uptime, CPU usage and Last reload. Config version identifies the active configuration revision, not its generation number. Section What to check Engine Engine version and build, API and instance information. Also shows start and configuration activation times and the Base or Full observability profile. Traffic counters Counter start time and coverage, as well as upload, download and connection counts. TCP and UDP counts are separate; the rate interval gives the measurement period. Memory Reported process and cgroup memory. The cgroup meter compares usage with a nonzero limit; a zero or missing limit shows no meter. Datapath Kernel attachment checks and degradation warnings, including state database failures. Includes program, hook and map checks and an attachments table. Backend features Features advertised by this backend. Select an entry to open its corresponding page. Features that are off Each limitation's cause, the setting or startup option needed to enable it, and a link to its requirements. Includes rule and group editing, import and revision history, and geodata settings. Appears only when limitations exist. Select Export state JSON to save the reported state. For absent fields or actions, see status requirements and reload, suspend and resume requirements. Status cards retain their space with placeholders while loading. Loading notices show progress indicators, and meters expose their names and value text to assistive technology.  Connections Connections opens on Traffic. Choose List to inspect individual connections; links to a connection or a filtered list open that tab directly.  Select a chart point or list row to inspect the connection. Its details show the outbound, chain and matched rule when reported. Use the outbound investigation steps to open the rule or run a trace.  Filters also search the outbound, chain and rule. Export CSV exports the filtered list. Read truncation and visibility notices before interpreting an empty list; the connection requirements explain coverage and which connections you can close. A row's add-rule icon is unavailable when the connection has no usable address or domain. More actions also offers Edit matched rule's outbound settings, View flow, Only this device and Close connection when supported. Close all with only device and network filters targets every matching live connection, including connections opened after confirmation. An outbound, rule or text filter, a truncated list, or an exceeded bulk limit restricts closing to the listed IDs. The action skips kernel-direct connections. Routing log Routing log shows recorded flows in Map and Records. It depends on flow recording.  Select a path in Map, then use its flow-count button to open the matching records. In Records, select a row to read its routing trace. Read the reason when a trace is incomplete. View connection opens the associated live connection if it still exists. Select Clear path filter to remove the pinned path. To create a rule from a recorded flow, use the add-rule icon on its record row; the detail panel does not contain that icon. Recording settings opens the recording controls. See runtime changes for their scope and lifetime. DNS The available tabs depend on the backend's query, cache and recording capabilities.  Tab Data and actions Statistics Summarizes the latest resolution-log page and cache information. Select a ranked domain to filter the log. Resolution log Select a row for the recorded request and answer. Export CSV exports loaded records, not the full history. Cache Filter cached entries by name and record type. Show expired includes expired entries. Read the confirmation before deleting matches or clearing the cache. Query Runs a diagnostic lookup. Follow the query steps. These lookups do not appear in the resolution log. To create a rule from Resolution log, use a row's add-rule icon to create a DNS request rule for the exact domain. If DNS rules are unavailable, it opens a routing rule instead. Choose Domain suffix to include subdomains. Cache filters support full names, suffixes, keywords and regular expressions, combined with a record type. A keyword matches anywhere: cdn matches cdn.example.com. The suffix cdn matches only cdn and names ending in .cdn. Filtering also works without deletion support. Clear filters resets the criteria and removes the domain filter from the page URL. When the cache reports memory-only storage, restarting clears its entries. The deletion confirmation shows the matching count, or the domain name and record type for name-based deletion. You cannot undo Clear all cache. No cache entries means the cache is empty; No matching cache entries means the current filters matched nothing.  Logs Logs displays engine log records. Check log recording requirements if no records arrive.  Use Level and Module to narrow the stream. Pause pauses display updates while the buffer retains only the newest records up to the page limit. Clear clears this page's records; Export downloads the received records, and Copy record copies one row in the same format used by Export. The page marks levels below the engine's recording level as not recorded. Change the engine level through Recording settings; selecting a lower display filter cannot recover unrecorded messages. A gap marker means replay could not recover some records after reconnecting. For messages from before recording began, use the service log. Events Events displays backend events, newest first. Check event requirements if the stream is unavailable. Kind starts at Exclude runtime updates. Choose All kinds or a specific kind, then select a row for its details and related links. Export JSON exports the events currently shown; Copy record copies one event in the export format, without the surrounding array. The list shows Time, Kind and Summary. Its toolbar reports connection state, retention limit and, when available, Resumes from the last position. Configuration activated offers View configuration when configuration is available; Flow records lost can offer View flow record and Recording settings. After reconnecting, replay can recover retained events. A gap marker means the earlier events are no longer available for replay.
